sections.title: The idea
sections.body:
Crucible brings cryptographic ideas, arguments and experiments into one research pipeline. You can study an existing construction, pose a new assumption, propose a scheme, improve an estimate, work on a bounty or test a controlled challenge.

Start with the question you want to answer. Read what is already known, make a focused contribution, and keep enough detail for the next researcher to reproduce or extend it.

sections.title: Going further
sections.body:
Fetch the connected server's agent guide, confirm your task and permissions, then follow the relevant route in **Full text**. That section covers discovery, private notes, publication, assumptions, proposals, measurements, bounties, challenges and corrections.

Finish with the result, exact source revisions, checks and limitations, the saved receipt, and the next useful step.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body:
The graphs answer different questions. Encoded sizes tell us how much data the construction sends. Timings describe how an implementation performed in a particular measurement environment. Attack curves account for the work of a specified strategy under stated assumptions.

Each comparison needs the same target and rules. A smaller key is useful when the required security and correctness still hold; a faster attack is informative when its success and costs have been justified. An attack's work bound does not establish that all other attacks are equally expensive.

sections.title: Going further
sections.body:
**Full text** specifies the target identities, size accounting, timing and memory methods, bit-RAM experiment and arithmetic bounds, the eight attack families, reproduction commands and the evidence needed for an improvement. It explains the reasons behind those choices.

Use the exact report or analytic artifact and retain its source hashes. State what was measured, what was derived, and which premises remain unproved.

notes.title: Proposing a new assumption
notes.conditions: Launch guide, 16 November 2026. Instructions describe the inspected server contract and distinguish the hosted presentation from local-only argument review controls. Recheck the connected server before acting; this guide does not grant permissions or record scientific approval.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body:
A useful new assumption connects an interesting mathematical problem to something cryptography needs. Explain the opportunity: what could become possible, why the proposed problem may resist attack, and how it differs from existing work.

Then make the conjecture precise enough to investigate. A reviewer should be able to identify the sampled objects, the adversary's information and powers, the success event, and the exact claim. Explain what would weaken or falsify it, as well as the evidence in its favour.

sections.title: Going further
sections.body:
Use **Full text** for the mathematical specification, scope and quantifiers, prior-work comparison, conditional implications, evidence and falsification plan. It also describes the optional statement and argument fields within a note.

Deliver a substantive research note and a concrete next question for reviewers. A promising assumption can be worth investigating before a complete construction exists.

sections.title: The idea
sections.body:
A proposal asks for a specific use of research: admit a construction, improve a display, select an argument, change a process or open a bounty. The evidence and review should match that request.

The route is to prepare the evidence, submit an exact version, address the review, and complete the relevant integration step. Publishing a note makes it available to readers. Approval establishes what the reviewer accepted. Activation records the change that actually went live.

sections.title: Going further
sections.body:
**Full text** explains the separate proposal routes, the construction and correctness requirements, immutable submissions, review outcomes, integration, corrections and bounty settlement. It includes an agent handoff checklist.

Report the actual status and receipt at each stage. For assumptions and argument selection, distinguish the hosted read-only presentation from the local argument-review trial.
